operationalization: The claim is a permission to treat simple programs as candidate rules for nature, alongside equations. No observable would confirm that such rules 'need not' be traditional mathematics or refute that they are 'equally candidates.'
obstacles: Any successful program model can be rewritten in mathematical language, so the contrast has no separating measurement.
Candidacy is a methodological status, not a variable with a confirming or refuting value.
rationale: The sentence is an epistemic claim about what kinds of rules are admissible in exact science. Fitting a program to one natural system would illustrate the method and would leave the permission intact either way. There is no public dataset whose variables are the legitimacy of a class of descriptions.

operationalization: Enumerate elementary cellular automata and other small rule spaces from simple seeds, and classify each space-time pattern as periodic, nested, or incompressible under a fixed compression and periodicity test. The claim is confirmed if a substantial fraction is not periodic or nested, and refuted if complex patterns are absent or confined to rules that are not simple.

candidate_datasets.name: Golly
candidate_datasets.role: open simulator for elementary and other one-dimensional cellular automata, used to regenerate the patterns

candidate_datasets.name: OEIS
candidate_datasets.role: published sequences generated by simple rules, including cellular-automaton columns, for comparison with the simulated output

obstacles: How often is 'often,' and 'as complex as any known' depends on the complexity measure.
Compression and statistical tests can miss hidden regularity.
rationale: The scope is the systematic enumeration of simple programs, which is a finite computation for the usual small rule spaces. Open simulators regenerate every elementary pattern in seconds, and a pre-registered classifier turns 'often far from simple' into a count. The superlative comparison with 'any known' complexity is the soft edge, and it does not block a yes-or-no test of the main quantitative reading.

operationalization: For a sample of physical and biological systems, identify the actual local rules and compare their complexity and typicality with simple programs, then ask whether those rules account for the observed complexity better than selection or continuum equations. A visual match between a program and a natural pattern would not confirm the claim.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: open 3D morphology archive; a restricted-scope record of biological form, not of the generative rules

candidate_datasets.name: FlyBase
candidate_datasets.role: Drosophila gene and expression data bearing on whether developmental programs are simple in the claimed sense

obstacles: Resemblance of output does not identify the mechanism that produced it.
Selection, reaction-diffusion, and continuum models can generate the same complexity.
The rules of most natural systems have not been measured at the relevant grain.
rationale: Existing morphology and developmental-genetics collections cover a few well-studied organisms and support case-by-case comparisons. They do not contain the generative rules of physical, biological, and other natural systems at the scope the claim states. A program that draws a similar picture is compatible with rival explanations, so current data can probe examples and cannot settle the general causal claim.

operationalization: Treat published predictive success as the variable: closed-form or numerically solved equations should predict simple systems such as planetary motion within observational error, and should lack stable predictive models for a pre-registered list of complex phenomena. The claim is refuted if equations routinely predict complex behavior to a stated accuracy.

candidate_datasets.name: JPL Horizons
candidate_datasets.role: public ephemerides for the planetary-motion clause, where equation-based prediction is claimed to succeed

obstacles: Failure of equations is easily confused with the current state of technique.
What counts as an equation, as opposed to a program or a numerical scheme, is contested.
There is no census of complex phenomena with a uniform success metric.
rationale: Horizons can check the planetary-motion half directly. The claim that equations almost inevitably fail once behavior is complex, and that program descriptions then succeed in a way equations cannot, needs a survey of models whose inclusion criteria are themselves interpretive. Published successes and failures are scattered across papers, so existing resources test a slogan's easy clause and leave the universal clause open.

operationalization: Fix four behavior classes (uniform or periodic, nested, apparently random, and localized structures) and apply them to samples of cellular automata, Turing machines, substitution systems, tag systems, and register machines. The claim is confirmed if the same classes recur across families, and refuted if some standard family produces a robustly new kind of overall behavior.

candidate_datasets.name: Golly
candidate_datasets.role: open simulator for the cellular-automaton families in the comparison

candidate_datasets.name: A New Kind of Science online
candidate_datasets.role: published rule diagrams and space-time pictures that specify the cross-family survey to be re-run

obstacles: Class boundaries, especially between randomness and localized structure, move with the chosen statistics.
The suggestion that the same classes govern nature is a further empirical claim and is not settled by the program survey.
rationale: The asserted finding is that the same overall forms recur across simple programs almost independently of the rule details. Those families are small enough to sample with ordinary simulators, and the book's diagrams fix the conventions. The hedged remark about nature is not the decision criterion for this computational statement. Fuzzy class edges lower operationalizability without making the comparison unrunnable.

operationalization: Derive a second-law statement from an explicit simple-program model, then compare its entropy production and equilibrium statistics with laboratory thermodynamic data and with the Boltzmann account. Confirmation requires a distinguishing prediction that the data favor; a simulation that merely increases a coarse-grained entropy does not.

candidate_datasets.name: NIST Chemistry WebBook
candidate_datasets.role: public thermochemical and spectroscopic data against which a derived second-law account would be compared

candidate_datasets.name: Golly
candidate_datasets.role: simulator for reversible cellular automata used as the program side of the proposed explanation

obstacles: Entropy increase in a typical reversible system is also predicted by ordinary statistical mechanics.
Resolving a conceptual difficulty is not a dataset outcome.
Coarse-graining choices can manufacture or remove an entropy increase.
rationale: Thermodynamic tables and reversible-automaton simulations both exist, so the computational illustration and the numerical facts of thermodynamics can be put side by side. They do not isolate this explanation from the Boltzmann and ergodic accounts, which predict the same increase of entropy. The claim that the program picture resolves the foundational difficulty therefore stays only partly testable.

operationalization: Use the standard definition of universality: a system is universal if it simulates a universal Turing machine, or an equivalent cyclic tag system, under an efficient encoding. The existence claim is confirmed by one checked simulation proof for a rule that can be stated in a single sentence, and refuted if every such proof fails.

candidate_datasets.name: Cook 2004, Universality in Elementary Cellular Automata
candidate_datasets.role: published proof that elementary rule 110, a one-sentence rule, is computationally universal

obstacles: Universality is relative to an efficient encoding of the input; a wasteful encoding would make the notion trivial.
rationale: This is an existence claim with a standard formal definition, and a published simulation proof for rule 110 meets it. One correct example covers the full scope. Reviewing that proof is specialist work on the scale of weeks, and the result has a stable published form that a small team can check.

operationalization: On a declared ensemble of non-simple systems, search for predictors whose cost grows slower than direct simulation, including closed forms, periodicity, and statistical shortcuts. A system is treated as irreducible on a finite horizon if every such predictor fails. The majority claim is confirmed only if that failure holds for most of the ensemble, which a finite search cannot fully prove.

candidate_datasets.name: Golly
candidate_datasets.role: simulator for testing whether elementary cellular automata admit shortcuts shorter than direct evolution

candidate_datasets.name: A New Kind of Science online
candidate_datasets.role: published examples of systems whose behavior is proposed as computationally irreducible

obstacles: Failure to find a shortcut does not prove that none exists.
Irreducibility of arbitrary systems is entangled with undecidability.
The ensemble of 'most systems' is open-ended, so small rule spaces are a subset.
rationale: Bounded prediction experiments on elementary cellular automata and other small systems are routine and can show that many non-simple rules lack obvious shortcuts. That is a proxy for a bounded horizon, not a proof that most systems are irreducible in the strong sense. Undecidability blocks a general algorithm that would certify the majority claim across its stated scope.

operationalization: The claim offers computational irreducibility as an account of free will. Free will, in the sense used here, has no measurement that would confirm this explanation or favor a rival compatibilist account.
obstacles: Free will is a philosophical predicate without an agreed observable.
Every deterministic and irreducible human-scale process is compatible with the explanation and with its rivals.
rationale: The statement links a formal property of some dynamical systems to a meaningful attribution of free will. No public dataset records that attribution in a way that would separate this story from other compatibilist stories. The claim can be argued and cannot be confirmed or refuted by observation or computation.

operationalization: From a universality proof for a simple system, derive a concrete undecidable question about that system, such as whether a given finite pattern ever appears. That settles the existence of Gödel-like limits inside simple programs. It does not settle whether those limits are relevant well beyond the current scope of mathematics.

candidate_datasets.name: Cook 2004, Universality in Elementary Cellular Automata
candidate_datasets.role: published universality proof from which undecidable questions about a one-sentence cellular automaton follow

obstacles: Relevance beyond the current scope of mathematics has no formal or empirical decision criterion.
Undecidability of one encoded question does not measure how often ordinary mathematical questions are blocked.
rationale: Universality of a simple rule is published, and undecidable questions about that rule follow by the usual reduction. That is the Gödel-like half of the claim, and it is checkable. The further assertion that these limits matter well outside existing mathematics is a judgment about relevance, and neither the proof nor any dataset decides it.

operationalization: Compare explicit program models with measured morphologies and with identified genetic regulatory mechanisms, on a pre-registered set of patterns such as pigmentation and branching. Confirmation requires a mechanistic match, not only a similar picture. A rival developmental model that fits the same images and the genetic interventions refutes the claim for that case.

candidate_datasets.name: FlyBase
candidate_datasets.role: genetic and expression data for Drosophila development, used to test proposed generative mechanisms

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: 3D morphological specimens against which generated forms can be compared

candidate_datasets.name: Golly
candidate_datasets.role: simulator for the cellular-automaton models proposed as accounts of biological form

obstacles: Pattern similarity does not show that the genetic program works as the model does.
Reaction-diffusion and positional-information models fit many of the same forms.
Imaging and genetic coverage is concentrated on a few model organisms.
rationale: Public morphology and model-organism genetics can test whether particular simple programs reproduce particular forms and whether the known genes do something similar. That is a handful of systems, not morphogenesis in general. Mechanistic rivals remain compatible with the same images, so the data support case studies and do not confirm that simple programs capture the essential genetic mechanisms.

operationalization: Take a list of sophisticated computational tasks and ask whether each has an implementation whose rule text is short, with task complexity counted separately from the initial condition. The weak reading is confirmed by one universal one-sentence rule. The engineering reading, including atomic-scale implementation, needs a demonstrated device whose physical rule, not only its abstract encoding, is extremely simple.

candidate_datasets.name: Cook 2004, Universality in Elementary Cellular Automata
candidate_datasets.role: proof that a one-sentence cellular-automaton rule can emulate arbitrary computation

candidate_datasets.name: Golly
candidate_datasets.role: simulator used to inspect simple rules that carry out definite computational tasks

obstacles: A universal rule shifts the task's complexity into the initial condition.
Atomic-scale implementation is an engineering prediction without a systematic public inventory of such devices.
rationale: Published universality shows that some sophisticated computations have very small rule tables, so the existential reading is checkable now. The claim that extremely simple rules are often all that engineering needs, and that they are implementable directly at atomic scale, ranges over technology that has not been catalogued in that form. Existing proofs therefore settle a weakened reading and leave the practical frequency open.

operationalization: Measure a declared complexity statistic along lineages with estimated selection intensity, in organisms and in digital evolution, and test the sign of the association. The claim is supported if complexity falls or stalls where selection is effective and rises where simple-program dynamics run without selection. It is refuted if selection systematically increases that statistic after the program-intrinsic contribution is controlled for.

candidate_datasets.name: NCBI Datasets genomes
candidate_datasets.role: public genomes whose size and gene content are crude proxies for biological complexity

candidate_datasets.name: Avida
candidate_datasets.role: open digital-evolution system in which selection can be turned on or off and complexity of evolved programs measured

obstacles: Genome size and morphological disparity are contested proxies for complexity.
Selection intensity is usually inferred from the same traits whose complexity is at issue.
Digital evolution tests an abstract analogue, not most biological complexity.
rationale: Genome archives and digital-evolution software let a team estimate some complexity trends with and without selection. Both are partial proxies: genomes are not a direct complexity measure, and Avida is not wild biology. Selection and complexity are statistically confounded in comparative data, so existing resources can challenge extreme versions and cannot show what produces most biological complexity.

operationalization: Evolve rule 90 from a single black cell and test whether each row equals the binomial coefficients modulo 2, equivalently the Sierpiński triangle. Equality at every row confirms the nested self-similar description; any mismatched row refutes it.

candidate_datasets.name: OEIS A001317
candidate_datasets.role: Sierpiński triangle (Pascal's triangle modulo 2) as integers, the row-wise encoding of rule 90 from one black cell

candidate_datasets.name: Golly
candidate_datasets.role: simulator that regenerates rule 90 for direct comparison with the binomial construction

rationale: Rule 90 is the elementary additive rule whose rows are binomial coefficients modulo 2, which is the Sierpiński triangle. That identity is a short proof and an immediate computation, and the sequence is independently tabulated. The scope is one fully specified rule and one initial condition, so coverage is complete.

operationalization: Generate rule 30 from a single black cell for a large number of steps and test it for global periodicity, nesting, and compressibility. The claim is confirmed if the pattern is not uniform, periodic, or nested, and refuted if a short exact description of that kind fits the whole space-time diagram.

candidate_datasets.name: Golly
candidate_datasets.role: simulator for regenerating the rule 30 space-time pattern from one black cell

candidate_datasets.name: OEIS A051023
candidate_datasets.role: published center column of rule 30, an independently tabulated slice of the same evolution

obstacles: The left side has persistent diagonal bands and the right edge is periodic, so 'almost no overall regularity' is a threshold judgment.
Failure of a finite list of regularity tests does not prove that no global regularity exists.
rationale: The rule, the initial condition, and the rejected alternatives (uniform, repetitive, nested) are explicit, and the pattern is trivial to recompute. Known local regularities, which the source text also notes, keep the phrase 'almost no overall regularity' from being a sharp predicate. A classifier aimed at the three simple forms can still confirm or refute the claim as stated.

operationalization: Exhibit one system with a short rule and a simple seed whose evolution fails periodicity and nesting tests over a long horizon. One such witness confirms the possibility claim; it is refuted only if every simple rule and simple seed yields a simple pattern under the same tests.

candidate_datasets.name: Golly
candidate_datasets.role: simulator used to exhibit rule 30, or another elementary rule, as a witness

candidate_datasets.name: OEIS A051023
candidate_datasets.role: independent tabulation of a complex slice of a simple-rule, simple-seed evolution

obstacles: A single witness uses one operational test of complexity; a different test could judge that witness simple.
rationale: The claim is existential: simple rules and simple initial conditions can produce highly complex behavior. Rule 30 from one black cell is a fully specified witness, and both simulation and a published sequence make the check immediate. Existence does not require a survey of every simple system.

operationalization: Inventory complex natural phenomena, determine the actual rules and initial conditions of each, and test whether most of them are simple rules started from simple states. Confirmation requires that causal inventory. Matching a program's output to a photograph tests only a proxy on a few systems.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: morphological archive used as a restricted-scope proxy for biological complexity, without the underlying rules

candidate_datasets.name: Golly
candidate_datasets.role: source of simple-program patterns for comparison with natural forms

obstacles: The generative rules of most natural systems are not known.
Similar-looking complexity is produced by selection and by continuum physics.
There is no agreed catalogue of 'most of the complexity seen in nature.'
rationale: The phenomenon of complexity from simple rules is computable, but responsibility for most natural complexity is a causal claim about the world. Public morphology covers a biased slice of biological form and does not record the rules that generated it. Existing material can support scattered lookalike comparisons and cannot confirm or refute the universal causal wording.

operationalization: Compute the first million center-column bits of rule 30 from one black cell, test that sequence for a repeat, and run a standard battery such as the NIST statistical tests. A repeat or a failed test refutes the claim; absence of a repeat together with passage of the battery confirms it relative to those tests.

candidate_datasets.name: OEIS A051023
candidate_datasets.role: published center column of rule 30 from a single black cell

candidate_datasets.name: NIST Random Bit Generation
candidate_datasets.role: public statistical test suite for binary sequences, applied to the first million center bits

candidate_datasets.name: Golly
candidate_datasets.role: simulator used to extend the center column out to one million steps

obstacles: Statistical tests can fail to detect regularity; passing them does not prove perfect randomness.
The outcome depends on which tests count as meaningful.
rationale: The non-repetition clause is a finite check on a sequence that is both published and trivial to recompute. The randomness clause is operational once a public test suite is fixed, with the usual limit that tests can refute randomness and cannot certify it. The scope is one sequence and one million steps, which existing computation covers.

operationalization: Compare rule 110 with rule 30 on the predictability of averages, such as density and block frequencies, using predictors that are cheaper than simulation. The claim is confirmed if those averages for rule 110 stay substantially harder to forecast while the pattern also shows persistent localized structures, and refuted if the averages are as predictable as rule 30's.

candidate_datasets.name: Golly
candidate_datasets.role: simulator for paired ensembles of rule 30 and rule 110

obstacles: Difficulty of prediction depends on the predictor class and the horizon.
Some spatial averages of rule 110 converge even when individual structures remain hard to track.
rationale: Both rules are elementary and fully specified, so ensembles of their averages can be generated and scored with ordinary statistics in days. A pre-registered gap in prediction error separates the claim from the rival that rule 110 is merely random-looking in the same way as rule 30. The word 'very difficult' still needs a numeric threshold, which is why discriminating power is only moderate.

operationalization: For the single-black-cell evolution, run rule 110 until the localized structures either die into a periodic regime or keep proliferating, and separately search for a closed-form shortcut that predicts that fate. Running answers the pictured case. It does not prove that no shorter method exists, nor that every initial condition is decidable by a finite run.

candidate_datasets.name: Golly
candidate_datasets.role: simulator used to evolve rule 110 from one black cell through several thousand steps

candidate_datasets.name: Cook 2004, Universality in Elementary Cellular Automata
candidate_datasets.role: universality proof implying that some questions about arbitrary rule 110 configurations are undecidable

obstacles: A successful finite run shows that simulation suffices for one initial condition and does not show it is the only method.
Undecidability for arbitrary initial conditions means a finite run is not always enough either.
rationale: The pictured evolution is short by modern standards, so the fate of that one seed is computable, and universality supplies a proof that no algorithm settles every initial condition. The sentence asserts both that one cannot tell in advance and that running as long as needed is the only sure method. Those two clauses pull apart under the universality proof, so existing resources test pieces of the sentence and do not confirm it as a whole.

operationalization: Evolve rule 110 from a single black cell, record the step at which a single localized structure remains in interaction with the left-hand stripes, and measure the temporal period of the resulting regime. Agreement with about 2780 steps and period 240 confirms the claim; a different survivor count or a different eventual period refutes it.

candidate_datasets.name: Golly
candidate_datasets.role: simulator capable of running rule 110 from one black cell well past 2780 steps

obstacles: The step count is stated as 'about 2780,' so a small shift in when the regime is judged to have started needs a tolerance.
rationale: The rule, seed, step scale, and period are all explicit, and a few thousand steps of an elementary cellular automaton are a routine computation. The period is an exact integer that either matches 240 or does not. Coverage of this single evolution is complete.

operationalization: In one cellular automaton, isolate a regular background and at least two localized structures with different velocities or periods, each a finite configuration evolving under the same cell rule. Finding those configurations confirms the claim; a rule in which every finite configuration produces only one kind of behavior would refute the general reading, and rule 110 is the stated example.

candidate_datasets.name: Golly
candidate_datasets.role: simulator for extracting the background and localized structures of rule 110

candidate_datasets.name: Cook 2004, Universality in Elementary Cellular Automata
candidate_datasets.role: published catalogue of rule 110 gliders and the periodic background they move through

rationale: The claim is that one shared cell rule plus different finite configurations yields qualitatively different collective behavior. Rule 110's periodic ether and its distinct gliders are a direct witness, regenerated by any elementary-automaton simulator and catalogued in the universality proof. The example's scope is fully covered.

operationalization: The claim explains a habit of thought by its origin in engineering practice. A survey of design methods can describe what engineers build; it cannot show that this origin is why the intuition fails, nor measure the intuition itself.
obstacles: The source of an intuition is not an observable with a refuting outcome.
Several historical origins are compatible with the same engineering record.
rationale: The sentence is a diagnosis of why a piece of common sense fails. Engineering artifacts and natural forms can be described, and that description does not identify the psychological source of the intuition or show that the diagnosis is the reason the intuition fails. The claim has no separating measurement.

operationalization: Draw a sample of natural systems with identified microscopic rules and estimate the fraction whose rules are simple and whose behavior is complex in the sense of rule 30 or rule 110. The claim is confirmed if that fraction is high on a pre-registered cutoff, and refuted if identified natural rules are rarely of that kind.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: morphological specimens providing a biased sample of natural form, not of natural rule tables

obstacles: Very common needs a denominator over natural systems that has not been defined.
Known rules of natural systems are few, and pattern resemblance is a weak proxy for those rules.
rationale: A frequency claim about nature needs a sample of actual rules. What exists publicly is a scattering of morphological case studies and a few systems, such as some growth and pigmentation patterns, whose mechanisms are partly known. Those materials can test a short list of examples and do not estimate how common the phenomenon is.

operationalization: Encode repetitive, nested, and rule-30-like classes as image statistics and search digitized historical ornament for each class. A clear rule-30-like ornamental pattern refutes the universal absence. Finding none in the digitized corpus supports the claim only inside that corpus.

candidate_datasets.name: Rijksmuseum collection
candidate_datasets.role: public collection of historical objects and ornament against which pattern classes can be searched

candidate_datasets.name: Internet Archive
candidate_datasets.role: digitized pattern books and historical art publications used as a searchable image corpus

obstacles: Survival and digitization favor some cultures and media, so absence in the corpus is not absence in history.
Stylized script and geometric craft can be misread as cellular-automaton patterns, and the reverse.
rationale: Open museum collections and digitized pattern books are large enough for a systematic image search, and a single convincing match would refute the claim that such patterns were never used. They are a biased fraction of historical ornament, and the pattern classes need an explicit encoder. The universal historical negative is therefore only partly testable.

operationalization: The claim says that studying simple programs yields fundamental scientific discoveries and that computers are not confined to evaluating equations. 'Fundamental' is an evaluative label, and once it is removed the remainder is close to a description of what computation is.
obstacles: Fundamental is an honorific without a confirming measurement.
Whether a mathematical finding about programs counts as a scientific discovery is a classificatory dispute.
rationale: That a computer can iterate a rule other than a traditional equation is built into the notion of a program. Calling the resulting findings fundamental discoveries adds an evaluation that no dataset separates from the rival evaluation that they are recreational mathematics. The sentence is methodological rhetoric.

operationalization: The claim states that the only way to find genuinely unknown phenomena is systematic, preconception-free experiment. A historical case of serendipity or of a theory-led discovery would bear on the wording only after 'unknown' and 'preconception' are given definitions the sentence does not supply.
obstacles: The only way is a methodological absolute, not a measurable regularity.
Preconception-free observation is not an achievable or recordable condition.
rationale: This is a norm for inquiry. Histories of discovery can be told so that they fit the norm or so that they do not, because the key terms are not tied to recordable variables. No public dataset decides it.

operationalization: Date the availability of interactive computers able to display large cellular-automaton surveys, and compare that date with the late-1970s and 1980s explorations. The chronology can support or weaken the technology clause. It cannot by itself show that missing computers were a main reason, as opposed to missing motivation to look.

candidate_datasets.name: Computer History Museum
candidate_datasets.role: public record of historical computing hardware used to date when large exploratory simulations became practical

candidate_datasets.name: Internet Archive
candidate_datasets.role: digitized contemporary computing literature bearing on what experiments were feasible before the 1980s

obstacles: A main reason is a causal claim confounded with the lack of a reason to run the experiments.
Some relevant machines and manual explorations predate the 1980s, so the cutoff is graded.
rationale: Museum catalogs and digitized technical literature can establish when graphics-capable machines made large rule surveys cheap. That tests the technological timeline. The claim that this absence was a main reason the phenomenon stayed unseen is confounded with the conceptual factors the same passage mentions, and those factors are not separated by the hardware record.

operationalization: Sample short programs and elementary cellular automata, and score predictors that do not simulate (closed forms, static inspection, small statistical models) against the true trajectories. The claim is confirmed if accuracy is low for most of the sample, and refuted if a cheap predictor usually matches the run.

candidate_datasets.name: Golly
candidate_datasets.role: generator of elementary cellular-automaton trajectories used as the prediction targets

candidate_datasets.name: A New Kind of Science online
candidate_datasets.role: published small programs, including register machines and substitution systems, that define a concrete sample

obstacles: Usually and simple need explicit cutoffs.
A predictor that secretly simulates the program would make the test vacuous.
Software-bug anecdotes are a separate, poorly standardized empirical clause.
rationale: The working content is a performance claim about prediction of simple programs, and a blinded comparison of non-simulating predictors with direct runs is a standard analysis on public rule families. Adequacy is limited by the open-ended population of 'simple programs,' which a stratified sample still represents at the strength the word 'usually' requires. The appeal to software bugs is illustrative and is not needed for the test.

operationalization: Generate primes by the sieve, which is the simple rule, and test prime gaps against a declared random model such as Cramér's. The claim is confirmed if several standard statistics match the random model over a long range, and refuted if the gaps are instead periodic or otherwise plainly regular.

candidate_datasets.name: OEIS A000040
candidate_datasets.role: the prime numbers, for direct statistical analysis of gaps and residues

candidate_datasets.name: The Prime Pages
candidate_datasets.role: public prime tables and records extending the range of the gap statistics

obstacles: Known biases, including Chebyshev bias and short gaps, mean that 'in many respects' can be satisfied while other respects are structured.
The random model has to be chosen before looking at the discrepancies.
rationale: Primes are an explicit sequence with public tables far beyond any historical sample, and comparing gaps with a Poisson or Cramér model is a standard computation. The soft quantifier 'in many respects' keeps the test from being a single sharp cutoff, while a finding of global periodicity would refute the claim outright. The data cover the number-theoretic scope the sentence actually has.

operationalization: Search the published record before the 1980s for a statement that simple programs systematically produce complex behavior of the kinds later classified. A clear prior statement refutes the priority claim. Failure to find one supports it only inside the searched corpus and under the chosen reading of 'identified.'

candidate_datasets.name: Internet Archive
candidate_datasets.role: digitized historical scientific and mathematical literature in which a prior identification would appear

obstacles: What counts as identifying the phenomenon, as opposed to exhibiting a hint such as the Game of Life or the digits of pi, is disputed.
Undigitized and non-English sources are missing from any practical search.
rationale: Priority claims are refuted by a single earlier publication that states the phenomenon, and a large digitized literature makes that search possible. The source text itself lists hints, so the boundary between a hint and a discovery has to be fixed before the search decides anything. Coverage of the historical record is incomplete, which blocks a confident confirmation of 'never.'

operationalization: Apply one behavior codebook (repetition, nesting, apparent randomness, localized structures) to samples of each program family named in the chapter. The claim is confirmed if each family lands in those classes and refuted if a family produces a stable overall behavior outside the codebook.

candidate_datasets.name: Golly
candidate_datasets.role: simulator for the cellular-automaton side of the cross-family comparison

candidate_datasets.name: A New Kind of Science online
candidate_datasets.role: rule specifications and sample evolutions for mobile automata, Turing machines, substitution systems, tag systems, and register machines

obstacles: Large rule spaces are sampled rather than exhausted.
Apparent randomness and localized structure are adjacent categories and can be swapped by the statistics chosen.
rationale: The claim is comparative and qualitative across the families actually surveyed. Those families have public rule conventions and can be re-simulated, the cellular automata with existing open software and the others from the published diagrams. A shared codebook makes the comparison confirming or refuting. Sampling and fuzzy boundaries are real limits and still leave a weeks-scale analysis that addresses the claim as stated.

operationalization: Evolve all 256 elementary rules from a single black cell and classify each pattern as fixed-size or unbounded, and as periodic or more complicated. The claim is confirmed if the shares are about two-thirds, one-third, and 14 percent under those definitions, and refuted if any share falls well outside that approximation.

candidate_datasets.name: Golly
candidate_datasets.role: simulator that enumerates all 256 elementary cellular automata from one black cell

obstacles: A few rules grow very slowly, so a short cutoff can mislabel fixed size versus unbounded growth.
Left-right and color reflections must be counted as the claim counts them, as separate rules among the 256.
rationale: The population is exactly the 256 elementary rules, a complete finite set, and the reported shares are approximate on purpose. A uniform cutoff and a periodicity test turn the census into an afternoon's computation. Edge rules with slow growth need a longer run, which does not change feasibility.

operationalization: Classify all 256 single-seed elementary evolutions with explicit tests for apparent randomness and for nesting, then cluster the positive cases up to left-right and black-white symmetry. The claim is confirmed if the clusters contain 10 random-looking rules in three forms and 24 nested rules in three forms, and refuted if the counts or the number of forms differ.

candidate_datasets.name: Golly
candidate_datasets.role: simulator for the full elementary survey from a single black cell

candidate_datasets.name: OEIS
candidate_datasets.role: independent sequences for well-known members of the survey, such as rules 30 and 90, used as anchors for the classes

obstacles: Apparent randomness is test-relative, so the count of 10 can shift if the statistical battery changes.
Fundamentally different is a symmetry classification and needs an explicit equivalence relation.
rationale: The integers 10 and 24 are claims about a finite, fully enumerable set. Re-running every elementary rule and applying a fixed randomness test and a fixed nesting test either reproduces those counts or replaces them. Subjectivity in the tests lowers discriminating power and does not make the census impractical.

operationalization: Compare behavior classes, and at least one numeric complexity measure, across elementary rules, three-color totalistic rules, and a larger-range sample. The claim is confirmed if the set of overall classes stops growing once elementary class-3 and class-4 rules are included. It is refuted if a pre-registered complexity measure keeps rising with rule complexity past that point.

candidate_datasets.name: Golly
candidate_datasets.role: simulator for elementary and multi-color one-dimensional rules in a matched comparison

obstacles: Class counts support the claim while absolute pattern complexity can rise with more colors or a larger range.
Beyond a certain point does not specify the threshold.
The most complex behavior is defined by the same four classes the elementary rules already occupy, which can make the test circular.
rationale: Cross-sections of cellular-automaton rule space are computable now, and they can show that the familiar four classes already appear among the 256 elementary rules. Whether adding colors fails to increase complexity depends on the measure: class membership and quantitative complexity disagree. Because those operationalizations compete, the general principle is only partly resolved by the available computations.

operationalization: Simulate all 2187 three-color nearest-neighbor totalistic rules from a single gray cell for a horizon of many thousands of steps, and label each as ultimately periodic or nested, apparently random, or structure-forming. The claim is confirmed if about 85 percent fall in the regular class, and refuted if the regular share is far from 85 percent once long transients are included.

candidate_datasets.name: Golly
candidate_datasets.role: simulator for the 2187 three-color totalistic rules

candidate_datasets.name: A New Kind of Science online
candidate_datasets.role: published examples, including long transients such as code 1599, that fix the rule numbering and the phenomena to be rechecked

obstacles: Ultimately regular can be hidden by transients of thousands of steps, so the horizon has to be long and the holdouts inspected.
A minority of rules may still be ambiguous at any practical cutoff.
rationale: The population size, 2187, is small, and each evolution is a nearest-neighbor totalistic rule that standard software already runs. The 85 percent figure is approximate and can be reproduced or missed by a uniform classifier. A few rules in the source itself resolve only after thousands of steps, which is still inside a weeks-scale rerun.

operationalization: Enumerate all 65,536 two-color mobile automata that update only the active cell, and test each for behavior beyond repetition or nesting. One counterexample refutes the universal clause. The extension, that complexity appears and is rare once neighbors are also updated, is a rate estimated by sampling the much larger neighbor-updating family.

candidate_datasets.name: A New Kind of Science online
candidate_datasets.role: published rule convention and sample evolutions for the 65,536 mobile automata and the neighbor-updating extension

obstacles: Nested versus merely long-period motion needs a compressor, and a weak compressor can mislabel a nested rule as complex.
The neighbor-updating family has about four billion rules, so its rate is a sample estimate.
rationale: The strict claim is a universal negative over a set of 65,536 explicitly defined machines, which is an easy exhaustive simulation. A single machine with incompressible behavior would refute it. The rarity claim for neighbor-updating rules is a sampling statement and is feasible on the same time scale, with the usual uncertainty of a sample.

operationalization: Sample generalized mobile automata, score the number of simultaneously active cells, and score an independent complexity measure. The claim is confirmed if complex outcomes are rare in the low-activity bin and common in the high-activity bin. It is weakened if the complexity measure is defined in terms of activity itself.

candidate_datasets.name: A New Kind of Science online
candidate_datasets.role: published examples of generalized mobile automata that define activity and the behaviors to be resampled

obstacles: Almost never and large numbers of cells need cutoffs that can create or erase the correlation.
If complexity is read off the same activity pattern, the correlation is partly circular.
The generalized rule space is sampled, not exhausted.
rationale: Activity and a complexity score can both be computed on a sample of generalized mobile automata, so a correlation is measurable. The result is sensitive to how the two scores are defined, and a definition that treats proliferating activity as complexity restates the claim. Existing simulations can estimate a carefully separated correlation and cannot yet make it independent of those choices.

operationalization: Enumerate all 4,096 two-state two-color Turing machines and all 2,985,984 three-state two-color machines on a blank tape, and test whether each space-time pattern becomes periodic or nested. One machine that remains incompressible past a justified bound refutes the claim; universal regularization confirms it.

candidate_datasets.name: A New Kind of Science online
candidate_datasets.role: published head-and-tape convention and sample diagrams for the two-state and three-state surveys

obstacles: Ultimately periodic or nested can fail to show up inside a short cutoff, so long-running survivors need a separate argument.
There is no single public table of all three million classifications; the check is a recomputation.
rationale: Both populations are finite and completely specified: 4,096 machines are trivial, and about three million three-state machines are a modest modern enumeration. A non-nested, non-periodic survivor would refute the universal claim. The remaining care is the word 'ultimately,' which requires a long cutoff and inspection of holdouts rather than a new kind of data.

operationalization: Sample two-color Turing machines with four or more head states on a blank tape, apply a fixed randomness classifier, and estimate the hit rate. The claim is confirmed if four-state rules yield on the order of five random-looking patterns per million and additional states raise that rate only slightly, and refuted if the rate is far from that or jumps sharply with more states.

candidate_datasets.name: A New Kind of Science online
candidate_datasets.role: published four-state examples and the counting convention for the two-color Turing-machine ensemble

obstacles: The four-state space has about four billion rules, so the rate is estimated by sampling rather than by a full census.
Seemingly random is classifier-dependent, and the same classifier must be used at every state count.
rationale: The numerical claim is a rate, about five per million, in a completely defined ensemble of four-state two-color machines. Sampling millions of short blank-tape runs estimates that rate to within the slack of the word 'about,' and the same sample design compares five or more states. A full enumeration is unnecessary for a rate, and the classifier has to be frozen in advance.

operationalization: Prove that a substitution depending only on a symbol's own color reproduces identical subtrees for every occurrence of that color, hence a nested pattern. The claim is confirmed by that argument, and refuted by one neighbor-independent rule whose evolution is not nested. Neighbor dependence is then necessary for anything beyond nesting.

candidate_datasets.name: OEIS A010060
candidate_datasets.role: the Thue-Morse sequence, a canonical neighbor-independent substitution output with an independently tabulated nested structure

obstacles: Rules that also depend on absolute position or on a global clock fall outside the neighbor-independent family the proof covers.
rationale: Neighbor-independent substitution builds the next string by replacing each symbol according to its color alone, so every symbol of a given color roots an identical subtree. That is a proof of nesting, not an open-ended search, and classical examples such as Thue-Morse are already public sequences. One non-nested color-only rule would refute it, and the construction gives no room for such a rule.

operationalization: Resimulate the published three- and four-color slow-growth substitution systems and test them for randomness-like statistics; that checks the existence half. For two colors, either prove that every slow-growth deleting rule is eventually periodic or exhaust a declared finite subclass. An incompressible two-color slow-growth example refutes the restrictive half.

candidate_datasets.name: A New Kind of Science online
candidate_datasets.role: published two-, three-, and four-color substitution rules with deletion, including the slow-growth examples to resimulate

obstacles: Block length is unbounded, so the two-color family is infinite and a search of short rules does not cover it.
Slow growth and simple repetitive pattern need numeric definitions.
The source presents the two-color statement as what the search found, which is weaker than a proof.
rationale: The existence of complicated three- and four-color examples is a finite check of published rules. The claim that every slow-growth two-color deleting substitution is merely repetitive ranges over an open-ended format and, in the source, rests on observation of the rules that were tried. Short rules can be re-enumerated now; the unrestricted two-color statement cannot be closed by that enumeration.

operationalization: Resimulate sequential substitution systems with three short replacements, starting from BAB, and test for incompressible growth; one such rule confirms that text-editor operations can be complex. The rate of about one in 10,000, and the claim that two replacements never get much more complicated, require the original distribution over rule lengths, which the sentence does not fully fix.

candidate_datasets.name: A New Kind of Science online
candidate_datasets.role: published sequential-substitution examples, including a three-replacement rule evolved for a million steps

obstacles: Randomly selected rules does not specify string length or the measure over rules.
Two replacements never is an infinite family once replacement strings may be arbitrarily long.
Seemingly random behavior is test-relative.
rationale: Particular three-replacement systems in the published figures can be rerun and scored, so the existence of complex search-and-replace behavior is checkable. The numerical rate and the universal claim about two replacements depend on a sampling scheme and a length bound that the claim does not state. Reconstructing a plausible ensemble tests a proxy for those clauses.

operationalization: Show that deleting one element per step walks through the string and rewrites each symbol by a block that depends only on that symbol, which is a neighbor-independent substitution and therefore nested or repetitive. Separately, exhibit one two-element-deletion tag system with incompressible evolution. The first half is refuted by a one-element tag system outside that reduction; the second by failure of the exhibited examples.

candidate_datasets.name: A New Kind of Science online
candidate_datasets.role: published one-element and two-element tag-system diagrams that state the reduction and the complex examples

candidate_datasets.name: OEIS A010060
candidate_datasets.role: Thue-Morse sequence, a model of the nested substitution behavior to which one-element tag systems reduce

rationale: Removing one symbol at a time and appending a block determined by that symbol reproduces a color-only substitution, just more slowly, so the nested or repetitive conclusion follows from the substitution argument. The two-element clause is existential and is settled by resimulating a published example. Both halves have a finite, checkable form.

operationalization: Simulate the published two-block cyclic tag systems from a single black element, subtract a linear trend of one half element per step, and run randomness tests on the residuals. The claim is confirmed if at least some of those systems pass, and refuted if every such system has periodic or otherwise plainly structured fluctuations.

candidate_datasets.name: A New Kind of Science online
candidate_datasets.role: published cyclic tag rules and growth-fluctuation plots that specify the systems and the trend to be recomputed

candidate_datasets.name: NIST Random Bit Generation
candidate_datasets.role: statistical tests applied to the detrended growth fluctuations

obstacles: In many respects random is relative to the test list; passing a battery does not prove randomness.
The trend of one half element per step should be fixed from the rule, not fit so as to whiten the residuals.
rationale: The systems are particular two-block cyclic tag rules, and their length sequences are ordinary string rewriting. Detrending by the stated average growth and applying a public test suite confirms or challenges the randomness clause for those examples. Because the claim says 'some' systems and 'many respects,' a single well-tested example carries the existential reading, with the usual limit of statistical tests.

operationalization: Enumerate two-register increment and decrement-jump programs by length, up to eight instructions, and classify each as repetitive, nested, or complex under a fixed detector. The claim is confirmed if the short lengths match the stated census (all programs through four instructions repetitive, two nested programs at length five, none substantially more complex through seven, and 126 complex programs among 11,019,960,576 of length eight) and refuted if those integers change.

candidate_datasets.name: A New Kind of Science online
candidate_datasets.role: published instruction set, program counts, and an eight-instruction example whose compressed evolution can be recomputed

obstacles: The count of 126 moves if the boundary between nested and complex programs moves.
Length-eight exhaustive search is large, though most programs die or cycle in a few dozen steps.
rationale: Every integer in the claim is a count over an explicitly defined finite set of two-register programs. An optimized interpreter classifies the short lengths quickly and the length-eight set, about 1.1 times 10 to the 10 programs, within the reach of a small team in weeks because almost all programs are rejected by a short cycle check. The soft phrase 'substantially more complicated' at length seven is the main source of classifier risk; the length-eight count is then a direct comparison with 126.
